https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: A staff presentation to the Troy Board of Education on the district's Schools of Choice (SOC) participation for 2023-2024, prepared by Assistant Superintendents Christine DiPilato (Secondary Instruction) and Kris Griffor (Elementary Instruction). It reviews Plante Moran Cresa elementary enrollment projections and 2022-2023 SOC data showing 285 elementary SOC students against 4,847 non-SOC students (5.55%), with Hill Elementary highest at 19.72%. A sibling-preference survey identified 13 kindergarten, 1 first-grade, and 17 middle-school SOC-eligible siblings planning to attend in 2023-2024.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
What it is
Slide deck of Schools of Choice (SOC) recommendations for the 2023-2024 school year, presented to the Troy Board of Education by Christine DiPilato (Assistant Superintendent, Secondary Instruction) and Kris Griffor (Assistant Superintendent, Elementary Instruction). Accompanying memo dated February 14, 2023.

Context
- SOC provides non-resident students additional enrollment opportunities; participation is optional and locally determined (application dates, grade levels, building assignment).
- Elementary enrollment projections supplied by Plante Moran Cresa.

2022-2023 elementary SOC data
- District total: 285 SOC students vs 4,847 non-SOC (5.55%).
- Highest SOC share: Hill Elementary 71 SOC / 289 non-SOC (19.72%); Wass 46 (10.90%); Costello 32 (7.64%).
- Lowest: Schroeder 1 (0.23%); Bemis 4 (0.86%).
- By ethnicity, SOC students were 64.91% White (185) and 15.79% Asian (45); EL 19.65%, Free/Reduced Lunch 15.44%, Special Ed 8.42%.

Enrollment scale
- Non-SOC students by grade totaled 11,428 K-12 for 2022-2023.

Sibling preference (survey of current SOC families)
- 13 kindergarten, 1 first grade, and 17 middle-school students (14 sixth, 2 seventh, 1 eighth) planning to attend in 2023-2024.

Purpose
Inform the board's annual SOC resolution on how many nonresident seats to offer.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
A PowerPoint presentation titled 'Recommendations for Schools of Choice, 2023-2024 School Year,' delivered to the Troy Board of Education by Christine DiPilato, Assistant Superintendent for Secondary Instruction, and Kris Griffor, Assistant Superintendent for Elementary Instruction, with an accompanying memo to the Board dated February 14, 2023. The deck explains that Schools of Choice (SOC) provides non-resident students additional enrollment opportunities, that participation is optional for districts, and that the degree and extent of participation - including application and enrollment dates, grade levels, and building assignment - are determined at the local level.

Enrollment projections were submitted by Plante Moran Cresa. Kindergarten and first-grade 'most likely' versus 'actual' figures are shown across 2020/2021 through 2023/2024 (for example, 2022/2023 kindergarten most-likely 807 including PreK versus 881 actual, and first grade 820 versus 741; 2023/2024 kindergarten projected 777 and first grade 821).

Data summary of elementary SOC versus non-SOC students for 2022-2023 (SOC / non-SOC / % SOC): Barnard 22/424/4.93%; Bemis 4/461/0.86%; Costello 32/387/7.64%; Hamilton 27/423/6.00%; Hill 71/289/19.72%; Leonard 25/372/6.30%; Martell 16/357/4.29%; Morse 7/402/1.71%; Schroeder 1/437/0.23%; Troy Union 11/409/2.62%; TSD Preschool 0/80; VLAC 0/49; Wass 46/376/10.90%; Wattles 23/381/5.69%. By grade: kindergarten 39/684, first 48/744, second 39/781, third 41/816, fourth 41/867, fifth 77/875; total 285 SOC / 4,847 non-SOC (5.55%).

By ethnicity, SOC students were 64.91% White (185), 15.79% Asian (45), 7.72% multi-ethnic (22), 7.02% Black (20), and 4.21% Hispanic (12), with one Hawaiian/Pacific Islander; the non-SOC population was 45.35% White and 39.94% Asian. Among subgroups, SOC students were 19.65% English Learners (56), 15.44% Free/Reduced Lunch (44), and 8.42% Special Education (24).

A separate enrollment-history slide lists non-SOC students by grade for 2022-2023 totaling 11,428 (kindergarten 859 including developmental kindergarten, first 722, second 779, third 812, fourth 835, fifth 913, sixth 896, seventh 868, eighth 854, ninth 924, tenth 995, eleventh 981, twelfth 990), plus a kindergarten/first-grade history back to 2009-2010.

A sibling-preference slide reports results of a survey emailed to current SOC families about siblings eligible for kindergarten, first grade, and grades 6-8 in 2023-2024: 13 kindergarten students, 1 first-grade student, and 17 total middle-school students (14 sixth grade, 2 seventh grade, 1 eighth grade) planning to attend. The recommendation memo describes the factors weighed - current enrollment, projections, patterns and trends, current SOC counts, projected age-eligible SOC siblings, and available elementary classrooms - and references using Fred Ignatovich's enrollment projection formula (most likely plus low, divided by two). Portions of the recommendation narrative retain earlier '2016-2017' template language, and the captured text is truncated.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
A bid summary tabulation for the Troy School District 2023 Paving Replacement Program, with a bid due date and time of January 30, 2023 at 11:00 AM. The work was divided into two projects: Project #1 covering Schroeder Elementary School, Leonard Elementary School, and the Transportation Center; and Project #2 covering Larson Middle School, Wass Elementary School, the Troy Learning Center, Barnard Elementary School, and Athens High School. - Asphalt Specialists, Inc., of Pontiac: Project #1 grand total $1,102,600; Project #2 grand total $1,037,475; combined bid if awarded both projects $2,140,075.

This tabulation is the comparative basis for the district's paving award recommendation under RFP 9953, which recommended Nagle Paving as the low qualified bidder.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
A memorandum from the Troy School District Operations Department (1140 Rankin, Troy, MI 48083; phone 248.823.4050, fax 248.823.4077) dated February 6, 2023, from Rob Carson, Director of Maintenance & Operations, to Rick West, Assistant Superintendent - Business Services, regarding RFP 9953 - BSSF Site Work, Paving Replacement & Slurry Coat Project.

Carson reports that an RFP was issued to obtain competitive bids for site work at Barnard, Leonard, Schroeder, and Wass Elementary Schools; Athens High School; the Troy Learning Center; and the Transportation Site. The scope of work includes removing and replacing existing pavement parking lot and drive areas along with concrete sidewalks at Barnard, Leonard, and Schroeder; removing and replacing paved play areas at Wass; slurry sealcoating at Athens High School and the Troy Learning Center (TLC) site; and excavation and stone base installation at the Transportation Site.

The RFP resulted in two bids, which were opened on Monday, January 30. Post-bid interviews were completed and conducted by Rob Rochon of PEA, Mark Paulus of Lecole Planners, and Carson himself. On that basis, Carson recommends Nagle Paving as the low qualified bidder for the Combined Projects Bid in the amount of $2,119,450.00, with a 6% contingency of $127,167.00, for a grand total of $2,246,617.00.

Upon approval, a purchase order would be issued to Nagle Paving. The transportation and slurry sealcoating portions of the project would be scheduled opportunistically pending site availability and weather, but most of the work would commence on June 19, 2023. Funding for the project would come from the Building Site & Sinking Fund and the Capital Projects Fund. The memo is copied to Donna Havrilla and the Purchasing Department file. This recommendation corresponds to the accompanying bid summary showing Nagle Paving Co. of Novi as the low bidder over Asphalt Specialists, Inc. of Pontiac.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: Board consideration item 7.B. for the February 14, 2023 meeting recommending which Troy schools be closed to open enrollment for 2023-2024. Administration recommends closing Barnard, Bemis, Schroeder, and Boulan Park schools due to enrollment and space constraints, and closing Athens and Troy High Schools, with one exception: up to 25 incoming ninth graders who reside in the Troy High attendance area but wish to attend Athens High may apply during a two-week window in March. The suggested resolution would adopt these closures.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
What it is
Consideration item 7.B. (Curriculum) for the Troy Board of Education's February 14, 2023 meeting: Schools Closed to Open Enrollment for 2023-2024.

Recommendation
- Close Barnard, Bemis, Schroeder, and Boulan Park schools to open enrollment, citing total student enrollment and physical space constraints.
- Close Athens High and Troy High to open enrollment, consistent with recent years' practice of maximizing building enrollment.

Exception
- Up to 25 incoming ninth-grade students who reside in the Troy High School attendance area but wish to attend Athens High School may apply during a two-week window in March.
- Students with siblings currently enrolled in grades 9-11 at Athens and Troy High may open enroll to remain for 2023-2024.

- Suggested resolution for the Board to adopt the above closures, with mover, supporter, and Yes/No lines to be completed.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
Board consideration item 7.B., dated for the February 14, 2023 meeting under the Curriculum section, addressing which schools should be closed to open enrollment for the 2023-2024 school year. Administration states that it reviewed enrollment for the elementary, middle, and high school attendance areas. Because of total student enrollment and physical space constraints at the elementary and middle school buildings, it recommends that Barnard, Bemis, Schroeder, and Boulan Park schools be closed to open enrollment.

For the high schools, the memo notes that the district's goal for Athens and Troy High has been to maximize each building's enrollment, which has resulted in both being closed to open enrollment for the past several years. Based on current enrollment projections for 2023-2024, administration recommends that Athens and Troy High again be closed to open enrollment, with one exception: not more than twenty-five (25) incoming ninth-grade students who reside in the Troy High School attendance area but wish to attend Athens High School. Applications for those 25 spots at Athens High School would be accepted during a two-week window in March.

The recommended action is to adopt the suggested resolution, which reads that the Troy Board of Education adopts a resolution to close Barnard, Bemis, Schroeder, and Boulan Park schools, as well as Athens and Troy High Schools, to open enrollment for the 2023-2024 school year, with the exception of not more than twenty-five (25) incoming ninth-grade students residing in the Troy High School attendance area who wish to attend Athens High School. The resolution further provides that students with siblings attending Athens and Troy High and currently enrolled in grades 9 through 11 will be allowed to open enroll to remain for the 2023-2024 school year. The document includes blank lines for the mover, supporter, and the Yes/No vote tally, indicating it was presented for board action rather than as an adopted record.

As required annually by state law, the resolution would authorize accepting applications for a limited number of nonresident students: 13 kindergarten, 1 first grade, and 17 total sixth- through eighth-grade seats at Baker, Larson, and Smith Middle Schools. https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
What it is
Consideration item 7.D. (Curriculum) for the Troy Board of Education's February 14, 2023 meeting: a Schools of Choice resolution under Sections 105 and 105c of Michigan's State School Aid Act.

Legal basis
- Michigan law requires a district to pass a resolution each school year if it intends to participate in Schools of Choice.
- Authority: Section 105 & 105c of the State School Aid Act of 1979, as amended by Public Act 300 of 1996.

Proposed 2023-2024 seats (nonresident students)
- 13 kindergarten
- 1 first grade
- 17 total in grades 6-8 (at Baker, Larson, and Smith Middle Schools)

Eligibility
- Nonresident students attending a school district within or outside Oakland County, provided that intermediate school district is contiguous with the Oakland Intermediate School District boundaries.

Action
- Suggested resolution for the Board to adopt, with mover, supporter, and Yes/No lines to be completed.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
Board consideration item 7.D., dated for the February 14, 2023 meeting under the Curriculum section, presenting a Schools of Choice resolution under Sections 105 and 105c of Michigan's State School Aid Act. The memo explains that, in accordance with Michigan state law, school districts must pass a resolution each school year if they intend to participate in a Schools of Choice program. It anticipates that a limited number of seats will be available for the 2023-2024 school year for kindergarten, first grade, and grades 6 through 8 at Baker, Larson, and Smith Middle Schools.

The item recommends adopting a resolution for Schools of Choice Sections 105 and 105c covering thirteen (13) kindergarten, one (1) first grade, and seventeen (17) total sixth- through eighth-grade nonresident students who attend a school district within or outside of Oakland County, provided that intermediate school district is contiguous with the Oakland Intermediate School District boundaries.

The suggested resolution reads that the Board of Education of the Troy School District, exercising the option permitted by Section 105 and 105c of the State School Aid Act of 1979, as amended by Public Act 300 of 1996, will accept applications for a Limited Schools of Choice program for the 2023-2024 school year for thirteen (13) kindergarten, one (1) first grade, and seventeen (17) total sixth- through eighth-grade nonresident students under the same contiguous-ISD eligibility terms. The document provides blank lines for the mover, supporter, and Yes/No vote, indicating it was presented for board action. These seat counts align with the sibling-preference survey results reported in the district's 2023-2024 Schools of Choice recommendation deck.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: A summary of updates to the Troy high schools' Course Description Book (CDB) for the 2023-2024 school year, a collaboratively developed OneTroy document revised annually through curriculum review. New courses added include Chemistry 1 and Chemistry 2 (with Chemistry 1 required for all students beginning with the class of 2027), a redesigned English 9 (also required starting with the class of 2027), Intensified Algebra 1 (being piloted at Troy High and Athens High), and Mindful Art. Chemistry 1 and 2 each carry a half credit that satisfies part of the math-related graduation requirement.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
What it is
Summary of changes to the high-school Course Description Book (CDB) for the 2023-2024 school year. The CDB lists course requirements and offerings by department; it is a collaboratively developed 'OneTroy' document (administrators and department heads from both high schools plus the teaching and learning team), updated annually through the curriculum review process.

Courses added for 2023/2024
- Chemistry 1: revision of the former full-year Chemistry course; required for all students beginning with the class of 2027. Grades 9-12, 1 semester, 1/2 credit, no retake; satisfies 1/2 credit of the math-related graduation requirement in the 12th-grade year.
- Chemistry 2: in development, launching second semester of 2023/2024; prerequisite Chemistry 1. Students seeking AP Chemistry take both Chemistry 1 and 2. 1/2 credit; also satisfies 1/2 credit of the math-related graduation requirement and is a prerequisite for AP Chemistry.
- English 9: redesigned 9th-grade English, required for all students beginning with the class of 2027. 2 semesters, 1 credit (1/2 per semester).
- Intensified Algebra 1: being piloted at Troy High (THS) and Athens High (AHS); covers all Algebra I content plus enrichment. Grade 9, 2 semesters, no prerequisite; scheduled with a math specialist; prepares students for Geometry.
- Mindful Art: new course designed with the counseling and art departments; 1/2 credit.

Purpose
Document annual curriculum revisions and new or updated high-school course offerings for students and families.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
A document describing updates to the high-school Course Description Book (CDB) for the 2023-2024 school year. The CDB shows the course requirements and opportunities available to students and is organized by department so that students and families understand the offerings. It is described as a 'OneTroy' document developed collaboratively by administrators and department heads from both high schools together with the teaching and learning team, and it is updated annually as part of the curriculum review process, with department teams determining where descriptions should be updated and where courses should be added or deleted.

Courses added for 2023/2024:

Chemistry 1 - a newly developed course, a revision of the previously taught full-year Chemistry class, required for all students beginning with the class of 2027. Grades 9-12, one semester, 1/2 credit, no retake; it satisfies 1/2 credit of the math-related graduation requirement during the 12th-grade year. Students study theories and concepts related to energy, atomic structure, bonding, chemical reactions, solutions, and combustion, developed through analytical problem solving of real-life phenomena and laboratory work.

Chemistry 2 - in development, beginning in the second semester of the 2023/2024 school year. Students who want a full year of chemistry in order to access AP Chemistry enroll in both Chemistry 1 and Chemistry 2. Grades 9-12, one semester, 1/2 credit, no retake, prerequisite Chemistry 1; it also satisfies 1/2 credit of the math-related graduation requirement in the 12th-grade year and is a prerequisite for Advanced Placement Chemistry. Content extends to atomic structure, bonding, chemical reactions, solutions, acid-base chemistry, thermodynamics, equilibrium, and gas laws, with a strong algebra foundation encouraged.

English 9 - a newly developed 9th-grade English course, a revision of previously taught 9th-grade English courses, required for all students beginning with the class of 2027. Two semesters, 1 credit (1/2 credit per semester); completion of both 9th- and 10th-grade English prepares students for future English courses, including Advanced Placement. The course emphasizes in-depth study of multiple reading genres and varied modes of writing and speaking, with frequent engagement with novels, short stories, poetry, nonfiction, mentor texts, and book clubs, and regular drafting and revision leading to literary-analysis, informational, argumentative, and narrative essays.

Intensified Algebra 1 - currently being piloted at Troy High School (THS) and Athens High School (AHS); it covers all Algebra I content plus additional enrichment to build background knowledge and ensure success in future high-school math courses. Grade 9, two semesters, 1 credit per semester, no retake, no prerequisite, scheduled in collaboration with the math specialist. It targets conceptual understanding, mathematical skills, and problem solving and reasoning, using visualizations and multiple representations (linear, absolute value, quadratic, rational, polynomial, power, and exponential functions) and metacognition to build students' positive beliefs about their abilities; successful completion prepares students for Geometry.

Mindful Art - a new course designed in collaboration with the counseling and art departments, one semester, 1/2 credit per semester. The captured text is truncated at this point.

The changes let the Board of Directors call a mid-year special election to restore director seats (Article VI), remove the "by June 15th" deadline for adopting legislative priorities (Article IX), require the Government Relations Committee chair to serve on the Resolutions and Bylaws Committee (Article IX), and restructure the treasurer's budget and year-end reporting duties (Article XI).
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
What it is
The proposed 2023 amendments to the Oakland County School Boards Association (OCSBA) bylaws, presented as "Currently Reads" versus "Would Read" comparisons with a proposed change and rationale for each. Word-document version among the February 14, 2023 Troy Board meeting materials.

Amendment 1 - Article VI (Election of Board of Directors), Section 1
Adds a sentence allowing the Board to call for a mid-year special election to increase the number of Directors. Rationale: lets the Board restore seats twice per year if necessary rather than only once.

Amendment 2 - Article IX (Committees), Section 4, Legislative Priorities
Removes "by June 15th" from the approval timeline. Rationale: move the process up so priorities are adopted by the GRC in the fall (Sept/Oct), sent to the Board in October, then to member districts for voting.

Amendment 3 - Article IX (Committees), Section 4, Committee Membership/Leadership
Adds: "The Government Relations Committee Chairperson shall be a member of the Resolutions and Bylaws Committee." Rationale: the GRC chair is not necessarily a Board member, and their involvement ensures the GRC's intent is reflected in resolutions.

Amendment 4 - Article XI (Fiduciary and Financial Responsibilities), Section 2, Financial Reports
Restructures the Treasurer's duties so the Board approves, no later than the June Board meeting, a budget for the upcoming fiscal year (July 1 to June 30), and, no later than August 30, the end-of-year revenue and expense reports.

Note
The extracted text shows some duplicated passages, an artifact of document conversion rather than additional amendments.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
The full comparative text of the four amendments proposed in 2023 to the bylaws of the Oakland County School Boards Association (OCSBA), formatted as side-by-side "Currently Reads" and "Would Read" columns, each followed by a description of the proposed change and its rationale. This is the Word-document version included among the Troy School District Board of Education's February 14, 2023 regular meeting materials.

Amendment 1 - Article VI, Election of Board of Directors, Section 1 (Number of Directors). The existing section provides that the Board consists of an odd number of directors, no fewer than 7 nor more than 9, with decreases accomplished by attrition (possibly yielding an eight-member board for up to a year) and increases accomplished by election under Section 4. The amendment adds one sentence: "In addition, the Board may call for a mid-year special election to increase the number of Directors." The stated rationale is to allow the Board to restore seats twice per year if necessary, rather than only once per year as under Section 4.

Amendment 2 - Article IX, Committees, Section 4 (Legislative Priorities). The Government Relations Committee reviews and revises its legislative priorities annually and submits them to the Board of Directors for approval. The amendment removes the phrase "by June 15th" from that approval requirement. The rationale is that the process needs to be moved up so that legislative priorities are adopted by the GRC in the fall (September/October), sent to the Board of Directors in October, and then sent to member districts for voting, with a suggestion that the voting period end by the start of the common calendar's school break.

Amendment 3 - Article IX, Committees, Section 4 (Committee Membership/Leadership). Committee members are appointed by the Board of Directors annually, may be reappointed, and elect a chairperson at the first committee meeting after appointment. The amendment adds a sentence: "The Government Relations Committee Chairperson shall be a member of the Resolutions and Bylaws Committee." The rationale notes that the GRC chair is not necessarily a member of the Board of Directors and that the chair's involvement is important to ensure the GRC's intent is reflected in resolutions.

Amendment 4 - Article XI, Fiduciary and Financial Responsibilities, Section 2 (Financial Reports). The Treasurer maintains all financial statements, reports, and budgets, distributing reports to Board members quarterly or upon request. The current text requires the Treasurer to present an annual budget (July 1 to June 30) by June 30 and an annual actual income-and-expense report by August 30. The amendment restructures item (b) so the Treasurer presents for Board approval: (1) no later than the June Board of Directors meeting, a budget for the upcoming fiscal year (July 1 to June 30); and (2) no later than August 30, the end-of-year revenue and expense reports for the immediately preceding fiscal year.

The extracted text contains some repeated passages, an artifact of the document's conversion rather than additional substantive amendments.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
What it is
The Oakland County School Boards Association (OCSBA) 2023 resolutions document ("Proposed New and Amended Resolutions"), listing the association's advocacy positions with adoption/amendment dates and cross-references to MASB and NSBA resolutions. Before the Troy Board on February 14, 2023.

Proposed new resolutions (2023)
- School Nutrition: supports expanding the Free and Reduced Meals program to include all children, as was done during the pandemic.
- School Safety: supports adequate state resources so schools can both educate and keep students and staff safe.

Proposed amendment
- School Finance Research Collaborative (SFRC) [Adopted 9/24/2019; Amended 9/11/2021]: supports reviewing and implementing SFRC recommendations, including studies on capital costs, infrastructure, and transportation, while holding higher-funded districts harmless. [MASB G 11.01; A-10.25]

Continuing resolutions (previously adopted)
Mental Health; Local Control; Evidence-Based Decision Making; Unfunded Mandates; School Aid (five parts A-E, including opposing vouchers/tax credits and enacting the School Aid Budget by June 1); Accountability and Transparency; Lame Duck; Universal Preschool; Special Education (full IDEA funding, noting the unmet 40% federal promise); Broadband Access and Devices [9/11/2021]; and Teacher Shortages [9/11/2021].

Also supports
The NSBA and MASB legislative agendas when aligned with OCSBA priorities.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
The Oakland County School Boards Association (OCSBA) 2023 resolutions package, titled to cover proposed new and amended resolutions, presented to the Troy School District Board of Education at its February 14, 2023 regular meeting. Resolutions state the association's official advocacy positions and are annotated with adoption/amendment dates and cross-references to Michigan Association of School Boards (MASB) and National School Boards Association (NSBA) resolutions.

Proposed new resolutions (2023). Two new resolutions are put forward. School Nutrition: OCSBA supports the expansion of the Free and Reduced Meals program to include all children, as was done during the pandemic. School Safety: OCSBA supports that there be adequate state resources to allow schools both to educate and to keep students and staff safe.

Proposed amendment to a previously adopted resolution. The School Finance Research Collaborative (SFRC) resolution [OCSBA Adopted 9/24/2019; Amended 9/11/2021] is amended so that OCSBA supports review and implementation of the SFRC's recommendations, including the recommended additional studies on capital costs, infrastructure, and transportation, and adds that while implementing the recommendations, higher-funded districts must be held harmless [MASB resolution G 11.01 and A-10.25 - 2021 amendment].

Continuing resolutions. Previously adopted positions carried forward include: Mental Health [9/24/2019] - increased mental health services and professionals in schools, and encouraging MDE to develop a model policy for identifying mental health issues [MASB G 9.01; G 9.05; G 9.50]; Local Control [9/24/2019] - support for community-governed public schools with elected boards [MASB A 10.10; A 10.55; A 12.70]; Evidence-Based Decision Making [9/24/2019] [MASB G 11.01]; Unfunded Mandates [9/24/2019] - opposition to state or federal legislation that increases district costs without full funding [MASB A 10.20]; and School Aid [9/24/2019], with five parts: (A) oppose using School Aid Fund dollars for anything other than K-12 education; (B) support additional funding for Special Education, At-Risk, and ELL students; (C) protect the School Aid Fund and local revenues from state tax policy changes; (D) specify in Michigan's Constitution that the School Aid Fund is only for Pre-K to 12th-grade public education and oppose private-school voucher or tax-credit programs; and (E) support enacting the annual School Aid Budget no later than June 1 so districts can meet the constitutional/statutory June 30 budget requirement [various MASB A 10.25 citations].

Additional continuing resolutions cover Accountability and Transparency [9/24/2019] for all school aid funds, including charter schools, cyber schools, community colleges, and public universities [MASB A 6.65]; Lame Duck [9/24/2019]; Universal Preschool [9/24/2019] - new dollars for universal preschool for all four-year-olds [MASB A 6.15(c)]; Special Education [9/24/2019] - full funding of the federal Individuals with Disabilities Education Act (IDEA), noting the appropriations have fallen short of the initially promised 40 percent of excess cost [MASB A 5.01; NSBA Advocacy: IDEA]; Broadband Access and Devices [9/11/2021] [MASB A-10.30]; and Teacher Shortages [9/11/2021] - statewide initiatives to address shortages and retain teachers, including incentives and easing Michigan certification for out-of-state teachers. https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: A staff presentation by Assistant Superintendents Kris Griffor (Elementary Instruction) and Christine DiPilato (Secondary Instruction) laying out Schools of Choice (SOC) recommendations for the 2023-2024 school year, delivered to the Troy Board on February 14, 2023. It reports that 217 SOC students (4.22% of enrollment) attended Troy elementary buildings in 2022-2023 against 4,920 non-SOC students, with Hill Elementary carrying the highest share at 16.57%, and summarizes a sibling-preference survey projecting 13 kindergarten, 1 first-grade, and 17 middle-school SOC students for 2023-2024. https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
What it is
A slide deck presented to the Troy Board of Education on February 14, 2023 by Kris Griffor (Asst. Supt., Elementary Instruction) and Christine DiPilato (Asst. Supt., Secondary Instruction) recommending Schools of Choice (SOC) participation levels for 2023-2024.

Program background
- SOC provides non-resident students additional enrollment opportunities; participation is optional and set locally (application dates, grade levels, building assignment).
- Elementary enrollment projections were prepared by Plante Moran Cresa.

Key 2022-2023 data
- Elementary total: 217 SOC students vs. 4,920 non-SOC (4.22% SOC, down 1.33%).
- Highest-share buildings: Hill 59 SOC (16.57%), Wass 35 (8.06%), Wattles 27 (6.46%), Costello 21 (4.91%).
- Schroeder, TSD Preschool, and VLAC each had 0 SOC students.
- SOC subgroups: Free/Reduced Lunch 24.88%, English Learners 18.43%, Special Education 10.60%.
- SOC by ethnicity: White 62.67%, Asian 17.97%, Black 8.29%.

Projection for 2023-2024
- A sibling-preference survey of current SOC families projected 13 kindergarten, 1 first-grade, and 17 middle-school students (14 sixth, 2 seventh, 1 eighth).

Purpose
To give the Board the enrollment data and methodology (Fred Ignatovich's 1.5 projection formula) behind the administration's SOC seat recommendations, which are acted on in companion consent items.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
A PowerPoint presentation delivered to the Troy School District Board of Education at its February 14, 2023 regular meeting by Kris Griffor, Assistant Superintendent for Elementary Instruction, and Christine DiPilato, Assistant Superintendent for Secondary Instruction, recommending Schools of Choice (SOC) participation for the 2023-2024 school year.

Program framing: Schools of Choice provides non-resident students with additional enrollment opportunities; participation is optional for districts, and the degree and extent of participation -- including application enrollment dates, grade levels, and building assignment -- are determined at the local level. Elementary enrollment projections were submitted by Plante Moran Cresa, showing 'most likely' versus 'actual' kindergarten and first-grade counts from 2020-2021 through 2023-2024 (for example, a 2022-2023 most-likely kindergarten figure of 807 against an actual 881 as of 1/27/23).

2022-2023 SOC snapshot (elementary): 217 SOC students against 4,920 non-SOC students, a 4.22% SOC share, down 1.33%. By building, Hill Elementary had the highest concentration at 59 SOC students (16.57%), followed by Wass 35 (8.06%), Wattles 27 (6.46%), Costello 21 (4.91%), Barnard 17 (3.96%), Leonard 15 (3.72%), Hamilton 15 (3.37%), Troy Union 11 (2.68%), Martell 10 (2.58%), Morse 6 (1.44%), and Bemis 1 (0.21%); Schroeder, TSD Preschool, and VLAC each had 0. By grade, SOC counts ran from 22 in kindergarten (2.71%) to 43 in second grade (5.23%), totaling 217 across preK-5.

Subgroup shares among SOC students: English Learners 40 (18.43%), Free/Reduced Lunch 54 (24.88%), and Special Education 23 (10.60%). SOC students by ethnicity: White 136 (62.67%), Asian 39 (17.97%), Black 18 (8.29%), Multi-ethnic 15 (6.91%), and Hispanic 9 (4.15%) -- contrasting with the non-SOC population, which was 44.00% White and 40.00% Asian.

Enrollment history: total non-SOC district enrollment was 11,428, with grade-level counts including 859 kindergarten (inclusive of TSD PreK / Developmental Kindergarten), 995 in tenth grade, and 990 in twelfth. A multi-year kindergarten/first-grade table traces counts from 2009-2010 (739 kindergarten, 817 first grade) through 2022-2023 (859 kindergarten, 722 first grade).

Sibling-preference projection for 2023-2024: a survey emailed to current SOC families identified siblings eligible to enroll -- 13 kindergarten students, 1 first-grade student, and 17 middle-school students (14 sixth grade, 2 seventh grade, 1 eighth grade) planning to attend.

The deck closes with a February 14, 2023 memo to the Board from Griffor and DiPilato citing the factors weighed in the recommendation -- current enrollment; enrollment projections, patterns, and trends; current SOC numbers and percentages; projected age-eligible SOC siblings; and available elementary classrooms -- and referencing use of Fred Ignatovich's '1.5' enrollment projection numbers under his recommended formula (most likely plus low, divided by two). Portions of the embedded memo carry legacy template language referencing the 2016-2017 school year and figures of 100 kindergarten and 30 first-grade applications, which do not match the 2023-2024 sibling projections presented in the slides.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: The Oakland County School Boards Association (OCSBA) 2023-2024 Legislative Priorities, a policy platform included in the Troy Board's February 14, 2023 materials. It sets positions across roughly fourteen issue areas -- School Aid, Mental Health, School Safety, Local Control, Unfunded Mandates, Special Education, Teacher Shortages, and School Nutrition among them -- including opposition to private-school vouchers, constitutional protection of the School Aid Fund for Pre-K-12 public education, and support for full federal funding of IDEA.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
What it is
The 2023-2024 legislative priorities of the Oakland County School Boards Association (OCSBA), included in the Troy Board of Education's meeting materials.

School Aid positions
- Oppose transferring School Aid Fund dollars to balance the general fund.
- Support added funding for Special Education, At-Risk, and ELL students per the SFRC Report and Lt. Governor Calley's 2017 report.
- Protect the Fund from state tax policy changes; constitutionally limit it to Pre-K-12 public education and oppose voucher/tax-credit programs.
- Enact the annual School Aid Budget no later than June 1.

Other priority areas
- Mental Health: fund services, wellness initiatives, and professionals in schools.
- School Safety: adequate state resources to educate and protect students and staff.
- Local Control; Evidence-Based Decision Making; ending Unfunded Mandates.
- Implement School Finance Research Collaborative (SFRC) recommendations.
- Accountability/Transparency for all publicly funded schools, including charters and universities (FOIA, Open Meetings Act).
- Early Childhood universal pre-school; full federal IDEA funding; broadband/device access; addressing teacher shortages; expanding free/reduced meals to all children.

Also supports
NSBA, MASB, and OCSA legislative agendas where aligned with OCSBA priorities.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
A one-page legislative platform titled '2023-2024 OCSBA Legislative Priorities,' produced by the Oakland County School Boards Association and included in the Troy School District Board of Education's February 14, 2023 meeting materials. It enumerates the association's advocacy positions across more than a dozen categories.

School Aid: Oppose transferring School Aid Fund dollars to balance deficits in the general fund; support additional funding for Special Education, At-Risk, and English Language Learner (ELL) students, meeting needs identified in the SFRC Report and Lt. Governor Calley's 2017 report; protect the School Aid Fund and local revenues from state tax policy changes; specify in Michigan's Constitution that the School Aid Fund is only for Pre-K to 12th grade public education and oppose any attempts to create private school voucher or tax credit programs; and enact the annual School Aid Budget no later than June 1.

Mental Health: Support and fund increased mental health services, emotional wellness initiatives, and professionals in schools as critical supports for safe school environments. School Safety: Provide adequate state resources to allow schools to both educate and keep students and staff safe. Local Control: Support local control of community-governed public schools with elected school boards. Evidence-Based Decision Making: Ensure education policy is evidence-based and research-driven to maximize each student's achievement. Unfunded Mandates: Support legislation to end unfunded mandates and determine the actual costs of legislation.

School Finance Research Collaborative (SFRC): Implement SFRC recommendations, including additional studies on capital costs, infrastructure, and transportation. Accountability and Transparency: Hold every school that receives public funding to the same accountability and transparency standards -- including FOIA requests and the Open Meetings Act -- covering local districts, ISDs, Public School Academies (charter schools), their authorizers and management companies, and all colleges and universities receiving public funds.

Lame Duck: Advocate for lame-duck parameters addressing accelerated passage of legislation after the November election. Early Childhood: Support universal access to high-quality pre-school for four-year-old children. Special Education: Support full federal funding of IDEA. Broadband Access and Devices: Expand access to quality internet and proper devices for all students and staff. Teacher Shortages: Implement state-based programs to address teacher shortages and retain teachers. School Nutrition: Expand the Free and Reduced meal program to include all children, as was done during the pandemic.

The document closes by noting OCSBA also supports the legislative agendas of the NSBA (National School Boards Association), MASB (Michigan Association of School Boards), and OCSA when those agendas align with OCSBA legislative priorities.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: A staff presentation to the Board on February 14, 2023 outlining annual updates to the high school Course Description Book for 2023. Three changes are highlighted: a new English 9 course, a new Chemistry 1 course, and a revised Team Sports physical education course. English 9 continues the district's workshop literacy model and aims to broaden access to Advanced Placement; Chemistry 1/Chemistry 2 responds to Michigan's 2015 NGSS science standards; and the Team Sports revision eliminates separate men's and women's sections in favor of a co-ed elective.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
What it is
A curriculum presentation to the Troy School District Board of Education (February 14, 2023) describing updates to the high school Course Description Book (CDB) for 2023.

How updates are made
- The CDB is updated annually to reflect curriculum and programming changes.
- Department heads work with curriculum and instruction specialists, counselors, and administrators; significant changes are shared with parents at Curriculum Night and during scheduling.

Key updates for 2023
- New course: English 9.
- New course: Chemistry 1 (paired with Chemistry 2).
- Updated description: Team Sports physical education course.

English 9
Part of a multi-year review begun pre-COVID; shifts emphasis from specific assigned books to developing skilled readers and writers, increases access to AP programming, and continues TSD's preK-8 workshop/responsive-teaching model. Supported by a partnership with the Teachers College Reading and Writing Project and literacy coaches at each high school. Parents can learn more at 9th Grade Parent Night at AHS and THS in March.

Chemistry 1/Chemistry 2
Responds to Michigan's 2015 adoption of NGSS Michigan Science Standards requiring all students to learn all standards (life, physical, earth science); a first step in revising graduation requirements so every student gets instruction across all three disciplines.

Team Sports PE
Historically offered as separate men's and women's sections; the revision makes it a co-ed elective and allows more sections.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
This slide presentation, titled 'Updates to Course Description Book, 2023' and dated February 14 (the title slide reads '2022' but the meeting is February 14, 2023), was delivered to the Troy School District Board of Education to explain annual revisions to the high school Course Description Book (CDB).

Process: The presentation explains that the high school CDB is updated annually to reflect changes in curriculum and/or programming. High school department heads work in partnership with curriculum and instruction specialists, counselors, and administrators to make changes. Significant changes are shared with parents at Curriculum Night in the spring/fall and again during the scheduling process, with counselors and principals available to answer questions.

Three key updates for 2023 are identified: a new English 9 course, a new Chemistry 1 course, and an updated description for the Team Sports Physical Education course.

English 9: Described as part of a regular review process underway for several years (begun pre-COVID). The rationale is that the current structure and coursework limit student options, and that all students should be prepared for and able to choose advanced coursework. The course moves away from an emphasis on specific books taught toward developing skilled readers and writers, increasing the volume of reading and writing and increasing access to Advanced Placement programming. It is framed as a continuation of TSD's preK-8 literacy transformation over the past eight years and its workshop, responsive-teaching model. Supports include a partnership with the Teachers College Reading and Writing Project for professional learning, a literacy coach at each high school, classroom observation and practice, and collaboration among colleagues. Parents can ask questions at 9th Grade Parent Night at Athens High School (AHS) and Troy High School (THS) in March.

Chemistry 1/Chemistry 2: In 2015 the State of Michigan changed the required standards for high school students so that all students must learn all standards under the Next Generation Science Standards (NGSS - Michigan Science Standards). A multi-year review found that TSD's existing high school course requirements did not provide all students with instruction in all required standards (life science, physical science, and earth science). Chemistry 1/Chemistry 2 is described as the first step in revising graduation requirements so that all students receive a common, consistent experience across all three scientific disciplines before choosing future coursework.

Team Sports Physical Education: Team Sports Fitness is a physical education course offered at the high schools. Historically two separate sections were offered during enrollment, one for men and one for women. Eliminating the separate sections allows both men and women to participate in the co-ed physical education elective and allows more sections to be offered.

What it is
The 2023 Member District Ballot from the Oakland County School Boards Association (OCSBA) on proposed new and amended resolutions, presented for the Troy Board of Education's vote.

Process
- The OCSBA Government Relations Committee (GRC) sets annual Legislative Priorities; the Resolutions and Bylaws Committee drafts resolutions from those priorities, referencing MASB/NSBA resolutions where aligned.
- Proposals are reviewed by the Board of Directors, then sent to member districts.
- A resolution approved by at least nineteen (19) member districts becomes the Association's official position.

Voting rules
- Each member district receives one (1) vote.
- Resolutions, priorities, and the ballot were transmitted Monday, January 23, 2023.
- Completed, signed ballots were due by 5:00 PM Friday, March 3, 2023, emailed to OCSBAboard@gmail.com.
- Per OCSBA Bylaws Article III, Section 2, votes are recorded on receipt of the completed ballot indicating the trustees' vote.

The ballot
- Question: 'Does the Board of Education approve the proposed new and amended resolutions as presented?' with YES / NO options and lines for district name, meeting date, printed name, and signature (by Board Secretary or Executive Assistant to the Board).

Contact
- Marc Katz, marc.katz@oakland.k12.mi.us, (248) 219-5949.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
The 2023 Member District Ballot issued by the Oakland County School Boards Association (OCSBA) covering new and amended resolutions, presented to the Troy Board of Education as part of the association's annual governance process. The ballot explains the underlying procedure: each year the OCSBA Government Relations Committee (GRC) establishes Legislative Priorities for the current legislative session, and the Resolutions and Bylaws Committee then reviews those adopted priorities and drafts resolutions based on them. Where there is alignment with Michigan Association of School Boards (MASB) and/or National School Boards Association (NSBA) resolutions, the MASB/NSBA resolution information is referenced. Once reviewed by the Board of Directors, the proposed resolutions are presented to member districts for consideration.

Approval threshold and eligibility: resolutions approved by at least nineteen (19) member school districts become the official position of the Association, as interpreted and pursued by its Board of Directors. Each member district receives one (1) vote on the proposed resolutions.

Voting period: the proposed resolutions, legislative priorities, and a written ballot were transmitted to member school districts on Monday, January 23, 2023. Completed ballots had to be received no later than 5:00 PM on Friday, March 3, 2023. The ballot stresses that it must be completed, signed, and returned to OCSBAboard@gmail.com before the deadline or the district's vote cannot be counted. It cites OCSBA Bylaws Article III, Section 2, under which member district votes are recorded upon receipt of the completed resolution or ballot indicating the vote of the district's trustees, and must be received before the stated deadline.

The ballot itself poses the question: 'Does the Board of Education approve the proposed new and amended resolutions as presented?' It provides checkboxes for YES (the Board approves all proposed new and amended resolutions as presented) and NO (the Board does not approve them), with blanks for the school district name and the meeting date, and a certification line ('I hereby certify that the foregoing is a true and correct record of the vote by the Board of Education') to be signed, with printed name and signature, by either the Board Secretary or the Executive Assistant to the Board of Education. Completed and signed ballots were to be emailed to OCSBAboard@gmail.com no later than 5:00 PM on Friday, March 3, 2023. Questions were directed to Marc Katz at marc.katz@oakland.k12.mi.us or (248) 219-5949.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
A slide presentation delivered to the Board of Education at the March 7, 2023 workshop, updating members on the Troy School District 6-8 mathematics curriculum and program review, situated within a broader K-8 review process spanning 2021-2023.

The deck opens by noting the district has used its current resources, Math Expressions and Big Ideas Math, for almost ten years, during which its understanding of effective practice has grown. It anchors the work in the 8 Effective Math Teaching Practices from NCTM's Principles to Actions: Ensuring Mathematical Success for All (2014) and lists the eight Standards for Mathematical Practice, including making sense of problems and persevering, reasoning abstractly and quantitatively, constructing viable arguments and critiquing others' reasoning, and modeling with mathematics. A belief statement, citing NCTM's Catalyzing Change in Middle School Mathematics (2020), holds that all students are doers of mathematics and that the program should cultivate positive mathematical identities so students develop deep understanding, critique the world through mathematics, and experience its wonder, joy, and beauty.

For the middle grades, the district is piloting two resources: the Connected Mathematics Project (CMP) and Illustrative Math (IM), both emphasizing task-based, inquiry instruction and enhanced access to the Math Practice Standards. A review rubric guides evaluation. Next steps in the middle school pilot include revisiting the review rubric, gathering pilot-teacher input via survey, and reviewing all collected feedback, teacher input, student input, student artifacts, and principal observations with the leadership team before making a final recommendation and planning implementation with all middle school math teachers.

The presentation addresses acceleration and middle school pathways, stressing that the current system does not lend itself to the district's deep-learning vision and that the emphasis should be on depth rather than coverage. The new curriculum is described as providing additional instruction in number sense and procedural fluency, richer tasks that elicit meaningful discourse, and multiple entry points that allow true differentiation in the general education setting. Students who wish to accelerate will have the opportunity to reach Algebra 1 by Grade 8 or before, and spring test-out will continue every year.

For family communication, the district planned to share information at each middle school's parent night: Baker on April 18, Boulan on April 19, Larson on April 24 and April 26, and Smith on April 25, and to launch a newly built Teaching and Learning website covering student pathways and how to advance. The deck closes with two extended quotations from Teach Up for Excellence by Carol Ann Tomlinson and Edwin Lou Javius, on valuing human difference, avoiding the underestimation of students, and operating from high trust, high expectations, and a high-support environment.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: A printed copy of the Association for Middle Level Education (AMLE) article "Creating a Culture of Connectedness through Middle School Advisory Programs" by Sarah Brody Shulkind and Jack Foote, included in the March 7, 2023 board workshop packet as supporting research for the district's middle school advisory proposal. The article argues that advisory programs build school connectedness, which research links to higher grades and test scores and lower dropout rates, and reports findings from a questionnaire study of three diverse middle schools with successful advisories.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
What it is
External research article from the Association for Middle Level Education (AMLE), titled "Creating a Culture of Connectedness through Middle School Advisory Programs," by Sarah Brody Shulkind and Jack Foote (printed 3/3/23). Included as background for the Troy School District middle school advisory proposal.

Core argument
- Advisory programs pair each student with an adult advisor and a small peer group for regular academic and social-emotional mentorship
- Such programs foster connectedness: meaningful relationships with adults, engagement, and a sense of belonging
- Connectedness is linked to higher grades, higher test scores, and lower dropout rates regardless of socioeconomic status
- Early adolescence is a critical window because the roots of alienation take hold then

Evidence
- Opens with quotes from four middle school students at a Los Angeles school describing how advisory helps them feel connected
- Notes prior empirical support and agreed best practices had been limited
- Reports a study across three diverse middle schools using questionnaires given to every advisor and student to identify which advisories fostered the highest connectedness

Purpose
Provides the Board with published rationale and research context underpinning the proposed advisory program.

A printed web article from the Association for Middle Level Education (AMLE), titled "Creating a Culture of Connectedness through Middle School Advisory Programs," written by Sarah Brody Shulkind and Jack Foote and captured from amle.org on March 3, 2023. It appears in the Troy School District's March 7, 2023 board workshop packet as external supporting research alongside the district's own middle school advisory proposal.

The article opens with an anecdote from an ordinary day at a Los Angeles middle school, quoting four students, described as a seventh grade girl, an eighth grade boy, an eighth grade girl, and a seventh grade boy, who reflect on the prompt "Does advisory help you feel connected to school?" Their responses describe advisory as making school less distant and more cheerful, giving every student from sixth through twelfth grade a shared bond with at least one trusted adult, and offering a place to unburden and refocus during a period when peers may face violence, drug, academic, or personal problems.

The authors define connectedness as a quality of school cultures in which students have meaningful relationships with adults, are engaged in the school, and feel a sense of belonging. They cite research associating school connectedness with higher grades, higher test scores, and lower dropout rates regardless of students' socioeconomic status, referencing sources such as Blum and Libbey (2004), Jackson and Davis (2000), Klem and Connell (2004), Mac Iver and Epstein (1991), McNeely and Falci (2004), and the National Association of Secondary School Principals (2006), and noting the Carnegie Council on Adolescent Development (1989) finding that personalized schools better prepare adolescents for adult success. They stress the urgency for middle-level educators because the roots of alienation take hold during early adolescence.

Advisory programs are defined as configurations in which an adult advisor meets regularly during the school day with a group of students to provide academic and social-emotional mentorship, create personalization, and facilitate a small peer community of learners, citing Cushman, Galassi and colleagues, Juvonen, and others. The authors observe that although advisory has been widely promoted and intuitively valued, empirical evidence and agreed best practices had until then been limited. To address that gap, they describe a study of three diverse middle schools with successful advisory programs, giving every advisor and student a questionnaire designed to identify which advisories fostered the highest levels of student connectedness and to surface the qualities of advisories and advisors that other schools might model. The extracted text is truncated before the full results. Because the piece is a published third-party article rather than a district document, it supplies the research rationale behind the accompanying Troy School District middle school advisory proposal.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: A March 2023 briefing on the Troy School District's elementary mathematics materials adoption, submitted by Natalie Haezebrouck and Julia Alder. It notes the district reviews curricular materials roughly every nine years, that the last elementary math adoption was in 2010, and that a new resource is sought to better address deep conceptual learning, number sense, and mathematical fluency aligned to the Michigan Math State Standards. A program-review timeline traces work from 2019 through 2022-23, including Math Recovery, MTSS development, and early adopters of the Bridges resource.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
A briefing document titled Elementary Mathematics Materials Adoption, dated March 2023 and submitted by Natalie Haezebrouck and Julia Alder, presented to the Board of Education at its March 7, 2023 workshop. (The extracted text carries substantial OCR noise, long runs of stray digits, around the readable narrative.)

Rationale: The document explains that in the Troy School District curricular materials are reviewed regularly, on roughly a nine-year cycle. Since the district's most recent curricular adoption, Middle and High-School Health in 2020, its philosophy of curricular review has evolved toward a comprehensive approach. Rather than simply seeking new materials, the district now takes stock of programming as a whole, including instructional practices, intervention, assessment, and current data, so that curricular, structural, and staffing needs can be aligned. The last elementary mathematics adoption was conducted in 2010, and the authors argue much has changed since then: a deeper understanding of the Michigan Math State Standards, the availability of better-aligned elementary math resources, and continued guidance on best practice from the National Council of Teachers of Mathematics (NCTM). In recent years teachers have been supplementing the existing resource with additions such as three-act tasks and number-sense routines to fill gaps; the district now seeks a new resource that fully addresses deep conceptual learning, number sense, and mathematical fluency.

Program review timeline: A graphic (Image 1, the Elementary Mathematics Program Review Timeline) lays out the multi-year path. In 2019, the district had Bridges early adopters, with a Tier 1 focus on conceptual understanding and modeling. In 2020, marked by COVID, the district worked to extend Math Expressions and math specialists and to support intensive intervention in math along with research resources for Tier 1. In 2021, staff reviewed TSD data and focused on math mindset, noting a trend of fewer students proficient in mathematics over time. The 2022-23 phase centers on comprehensive math program development, developing a Multi-Tiered System of Supports (MTSS), and learning and implementing Math Recovery and Tier 1 research in research classrooms. Together the document builds the case, on both data and best-practice grounds, for adopting refreshed elementary mathematics materials, complementing the separate 6-8 math review presented at the same workshop.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: A March 7, 2023 Advisory Committee presentation proposing a middle school advisory program for the Troy School District, justified in part by the district's 2021-22 Middle School Connected Survey. Under the plan every student would be assigned a grade-level advisory and every teacher an advisory class, meeting twice per week in 25-minute sessions around a shared social-emotional learning curriculum. Curriculum development and grade-level leadership would be handled through posted paid positions and stipends.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
What it is
Advisory Committee presentation to the Board, dated March 7, 2023, proposing a middle school advisory program for the Troy School District.

Purpose of advisory
- Give students and staff a safe space to build meaningful relationships, develop social-emotional skills, elevate student voice, and foster a sense of belonging

Rationale
- Need supported by the TSD Middle School Connected Survey from the 2021-22 school year

Who is involved
- Every student assigned an advisory period, placed by grade level with consideration for need
- All teaching staff assigned an advisory class
- Counselors, administrators, categorical teachers, social workers, and a psychologist assigned as classroom partners for support and emergencies

Structure and content
- Meets twice per week in 25-minute sessions, grouped by grade level
- Common social-emotional learning curriculum across all middle schools, with building-level flexibility

Staffing
- Paid summer positions posted to develop/select curriculum, multiple per grade level for cross-building collaboration
- Building grade-level leaders supported by paid stipends during the year

Purpose
Seeks Board support for launching a consistent, district-wide middle school advisory model.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
A slide presentation from the Advisory Committee, dated March 7, 2023, proposing the creation of a middle school advisory program in the Troy School District, delivered at the Board of Education workshop.

The deck defines the purpose of advisory as providing students and staff a safe space to build meaningful relationships; develop social-emotional skills such as personal growth, confidence, sense of self, balance, and resilience; elevate student voice; and foster a sense of belonging for all within the school community. This purpose statement is repeated for emphasis across the slides.

To establish need, the committee points to data from the TSD Middle School Connected Survey conducted during the 2021-22 school year, with slides titled "Does the TSD Need Advisory?" and "What the Data Says" (the underlying charts are not captured in the extracted text).

On participation, the proposal states that all students will be assigned an advisory period, placed by grade level, with consideration given to students based on need, and that all teaching staff will be assigned an advisory class. Counselors, administrators, categorical teachers, social workers, a psychologist, and other ancillary staff will be assigned as partners to classrooms so they are available for emergencies and additional support throughout the building.

Regarding content, the advisory curriculum will focus on social-emotional learning, and all middle schools will use the same curriculum, with variety and flexibility to support the unique needs of each building. Structurally, advisory would meet twice per week in 25-minute sessions, with students grouped by grade level.

For materials and staffing, the plan calls for positions to be posted for the development and selection of advisory curriculum over the summer as a paid position, with multiple positions per grade level so that teams can collaborate across buildings to develop consistent resources. Each building would also identify grade-level leaders, supported by paid stipends, to sustain advisory at each grade level throughout the year. The presentation closes with a questions slide. It is paired in the same workshop packet with the AMLE research article on advisory and connectedness, which supplies the supporting rationale.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
A PowerPoint presentation titled "Partnership Proposal," delivered to the Troy School District (TSD) Board of Education Workshop on March 7, 2023, laying out a proposed partnership between the district and the Troy Racquet Club (TRC) to expand tennis-court capacity in Troy.

Objective and challenge. The stated objective is to increase the capacity of quality tennis courts in Troy. The presentation frames the problem as a shortage of tennis courts in the city, a situation it says worsened after middle school courts were removed in summer 2019.

Estimated usage: approximately 1,000 members; tennis classes serving 320-340 students per eight-week session; more than 500 users of member court time and lessons; roughly 350 USTA league players; and 130+ pickleball players.

Benefits for the district. The proposal lists an approximately $1.2 million cost avoidance for TSD. It argues that a tennis center on campus would complement the district's academic and fine-arts strengths, set a high standard statewide, and emphasize that Troy is a "tennis town." It stresses that both Athens and Troy High tennis programs would gain the same access to the facility, addressing the difficulty of securing indoor court time during the spring season, especially for JV programs, and giving TSD tennis programs a competitive advantage. It also notes PE classes could use the facility during the school day for tennis and pickleball sections, with the possibility of TRC providing a pro to assist PE teachers.

Structure and next step. Slides 9 through 13 are headed "Responses to TSD Board Member Questions" (continued), indicating the deck addressed earlier board inquiries, though the specific answers are not captured in the extracted text. No lease terms, dollar figures beyond the cited cost avoidance, or final vote are recorded in this document; it is a proposal seeking authorization to negotiate.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
What it is
A "Discovery Report" by education-design firm Fielding International for Troy School District (TSD), part of a visioning process to re-imagine the middle school experience; among materials for the March 7, 2023 Board of Education Workshop.

Future priorities of Troy leaders
Organized around pillars such as Early Childhood to Career, Student-Driven Learning, a schedule resembling a modern workplace, programs accessible to all students, Equity and Well-Being, Connection and Pride, fresh learning spaces with natural light, Deep Learning, and building the capacity of students, staff, and families.

Vision statements (6)
1. Innovative uses of space and technology that adapt to future program.
2. A student sense of belonging and pride inspired by meaningful relationships.
3. Students as agents of their own learning.
4. The practice and understanding of collaboration among students, teachers, and community.
5. Consistently improved teaching and learning.
6. Whole-child wellness at the center.

Observed challenges
- Environment: technology siloed in single rooms; inflexible furniture; lack of natural/controllable light; rigid cafeterias; underutilized media centers; hallways used for breakout; limited individual-project space.
- Program: technology often mimicking traditional strategies; "templated" activities limiting voice and choice; large-group instruction far more prevalent than other strategies.

Schools observed
Baker, Boulan Park, Smith, and Boyd R. Larson middle schools.

Teacher input
Collaboration happens informally (hallways, before/after school) rather than by planned grade-level time; limited shared understanding of the "6 C's"; classroom technology use largely in the "Augmentation" band of the SAMR model.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
A "Discovery Report" produced by Fielding International (tagline "Designing schools where learners thrive") for the Troy School District (TSD), documenting the opening discovery phase of a visioning process to re-imagine the district's middle schools. It was among the materials before the Board of Education Workshop on March 7, 2023.

Future priorities. The report maps priorities of Troy leaders against a set of pillars: Early Childhood to Career; Student-Driven Learning; a schedule that resembles a modern workplace; programs accessible to all students; Equity and Well-Being; Connection and Pride; fresh learning spaces; natural light; Deep Learning; collaboration to solve meaningful problems; room to adapt; high levels of student achievement with authentic measures; and building the capacity of students, staff, and families, including increased student/teacher collaboration and families visiting schools to observe programs.

Vision for the future. The path forward is described as including student voice, clearly defined goals, community involvement, equity and inclusion, a collective vision of what could be, excitement, and shifts in pedagogy. Six numbered vision statements answer "Who do we want to be?": (1) innovative uses of space and technology that can adapt to future program; (2) a student sense of belonging and pride inspired by meaningful relationships; (3) students as agents of their own learning; (4) the practice and understanding of collaboration among students, teachers, and community; (5) consistently improved teaching and learning; and (6) whole-child wellness at the center.

Challenges in the observed environment. The report catalogs physical-environment issues: technology accumulated in single rooms rather than integrated; inflexible furniture that limits agility; lack of natural and/or controllable lighting; rigid cafeteria design limiting utilization; underutilized media centers; hallways used for breakout with no informal student spaces; and limited space for individual projects and learning support.

Challenges in the observed program. Instructional observations include technology use often mimicking traditional strategies; classroom features that limit experience variety; challenging outdoor connections that may limit use; "templated" activities that limit autonomy, voice, and choice; and large-group instruction being far more prevalent than other strategies (an inquiry-based rating of 2.4 is noted).

School snapshots. The report presents "snapshots in time" of the district's four middle schools: Baker Middle School, Boulan Park Middle School, Smith Middle School, and Boyd R. Larson Middle School.

What teachers said. Teacher conversation notes indicate collaboration is fit into schedules as needed and occurs informally in hallways, in one another's rooms, and before or after school, largely within departments rather than by grade level, because the schedule does not allow shared planning time. On the "6 C's," teachers referenced benchmark assessments in math and English, which the report reads as a lack of shared understanding of the competencies or of how to teach skills like collaboration explicitly. On "Tech for Transformation," iPad-use examples fell into the Augmentation band of the SAMR model, and the report notes the technology teacher did not seem familiar with the SAMR framework. The document is diagnostic, establishing a baseline rather than recommending specific construction or budget actions.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: A companion "Learning Ecosystem Report" prepared by Fielding International for Troy School District, articulating a proposed mission for a re-imagined middle school experience built on seven aims: experiential and authentic learning, engagement and fun, cultural competencies, social-emotional learning and empathy, future-ready skills, relationships and community, and encouraging healthy risks. For each aim it summarizes what students and staff say it means and how it would look and feel. Presented at the March 7, 2023 board workshop.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
What it is
A "Learning Ecosystem Report" by Fielding International for Troy School District (TSD), extending the middle school visioning work; among materials for the March 7, 2023 Board of Education Workshop.

Proposed middle school mission (7 aims)
1. Provide experiential and authentic learning.
2. Strive for engagement and fun.
3. Foster cultural competencies.
4. Promote social-emotional learning and empathy.
5. Cultivate future-ready skills.
6. Build relationships, community, and connectedness.
7. Encourage healthy risks.

How it is structured
For each aim, a table captures separate student and staff answers to three prompts: "What does this mean?", "What would we hear or see?", and "What would it feel like?"

Representative content
- Experiential/authentic learning: learning tied to the outside world, field trips and guest speakers, moving away from lecture, flexibility in assessment; would feel liberating and give ownership.
- Engagement and fun: a "menu" of options, choice and voice, hands-on and project-based learning, a lighter homework load; teacher as partner, coach, or mentor.
- Cultural competencies: exposure to varied cultures, representation in curriculum, culturally responsive teaching, diverse groupings; increased sense of belonging and empathy.
- Social-emotional learning: safe environments, explicitly taught character traits, mindfulness, staff check-ins; feeling supported, safe, seen and heard.
- Future-ready skills: trying new things, process over product, changed assessment practices, cross-curricular ownership; more autonomy and pride.

Purpose
Translates the visioning work into a mission framework grounded in student and staff voice; aspirational and diagnostic rather than a budget or construction plan.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
A "Learning Ecosystem Report" prepared by Fielding International ("Designing schools where learners thrive") for the Troy School District (TSD), continuing the firm's middle school visioning engagement and included among materials for the March 7, 2023 Board of Education Workshop. Where the companion Discovery Report diagnoses current conditions, this report frames a proposed mission for a re-imagined middle school and grounds it in the voices of students and staff.

Proposed mission. The report asks what the mission of a re-imagined middle school experience might be and answers with seven elements: (1) provide experiential and authentic learning; (2) strive for engagement and fun; (3) foster cultural competencies; (4) promote social-emotional learning and empathy; (5) cultivate future-ready skills; (6) build relationships, community, and connectedness; and (7) encourage healthy risks.

Method. For each mission element the document presents a table with two columns, Students and Staff, responding to three questions: "What does this mean?", "What would we hear or see?", and "What would it feel like?" This structure surfaces how each group interprets the aim.

Representative content by element. For experiential and authentic learning, responses include learning that relates to the outside world, field trips and guest speakers, students "becoming the expert," stepping away from lecture, simulation experiences, and flexibility in assessment; the feeling is described as liberating, with ownership and value, though staff note potential stress from planning and coordination. For engagement and fun, ideas include a "menu" of options, choice and voice, hands-on activities, a lighter homework load, field trips, and project- or problem-based learning centered on student voice and choice, with the teacher acting as partner, coach, or mentor and assessments changing; it would feel fun, engaging, motivating, and welcoming, if slightly more anxious given the growth expected. For fostering cultural competencies, responses cite exposure to various cultures, representation in curriculum and building images, culturally responsive teaching, more diverse staff, working in diverse groupings, and healthy discourse; it would feel like being seen, with an increased sense of belonging, safety, inclusion, and empathy. For social-emotional learning and empathy, responses include environments where students feel safe and ready to learn, opportunities to explore other points of view, explicitly taught character traits and values, mindfulness strategies, proper training and research-based supports for staff, adults available to talk to, a common language of respect, dedicated spaces, and "recess" time; it would feel inclusive, supported, refreshed, safe, valued, seen, and heard. For cultivating future-ready skills, responses emphasize trying new things, knowing strategies for learning, fewer siloed experiences, prioritizing process over product, changes in assessment practices, cross-curricular ownership of teaching, and professional learning; it would feel more autonomous, authentic, and full of ownership and pride, while normalizing being at a different place, rate, or age.

Purpose. The report translates the district's visioning work into an actionable mission framework built from stakeholder input. It is aspirational and diagnostic in nature and does not contain budget figures, vote outcomes, or construction commitments.

Typical heights
- Distinct height sets are specified for K-2nd grade classrooms and for 3rd-12th grade classrooms, spanning Pre-K through 12.

Table and chair kits
- Kit 1a: VS Tano Stacking Table (asymmetrical polygon), four tables 27 by 26 inches, fixed height, plus four four-leg chairs; seat height 16.5 to 21.5 inches; shares bins with Kits 7a and 2a.
