https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
Prepared for the Troy School District and dated February 8, 2023, this guide presents the furniture design kits being evaluated for the district's 2023 pilot classroom program. It explains that staff feelings about color and finishes will be gathered at Workshop #2 and factored into final color selections with the Executive team, and that the professional and executive teams will size furniture according to grade level, with typical heights spanning Pre-K through 12th grade and distinct height sets defined for K-2nd grade and for 3rd-12th grade classrooms. The kits are described as designed with variety in mind, offering individual, two-person, and four-person seating.

Kit 1a is a single-student configuration built around the VS Tano Stacking Table (an asymmetrical polygon table), including four tables measuring 27 by 26 inches with fixed height, two glides plus two casters, and four four-leg chairs with glides; seat height adjusts from 16.5 to 21.5 inches, and the tables carry bins that can be used with those in Kits 7a and 2a. Kit 1b uses the VS Shift + Thumbprint Stacking Table, pairing two convex tables and two concave tables (each 21 by 38 inches) with four chairs; it shares a radius with Kit 4d and Ancillary Kit 6b and is noted as the largest single-student table for learners needing more space. Kit 1c uses the VS Lite Stacking Table (rectangle), with four tables 21 by 27 inches plus four chairs, and is highlighted as a stacking solution to clear floor space.

Kit 2a is a two-top VS Eco Table (rectangle) with two height-adjustable tables 20 by 52 inches (23 to 32 inches, a set-it-and-forget-it leg adjustment) and four chairs, suggested as a standing-height solution for lower elementary students or wheelchair users. Kit 2b is a two-top Fleetwood Plane Unitized Frame Table with two tables 24 by 60 inches on four casters, height-adjustable 23 to 32 inches, plus four four-leg chairs, described as a standard size for two older students and well suited to secondary classrooms, with optional table shelf and backpack hook and a lounge concept referenced in Kit 6c. Kit 2c is a two-top standing version of the Fleetwood Plane table, two tables 24 by 60 inches with a foot rail, height-adjustable 34 to 42 inches, paired with four adjustable five-star stools whose seat height ranges from 20.5 to 30.75 inches.

Throughout, three chair mobility options recur: four-leg with glides (identified as a K-1st grade option), four-leg with casters (a K-12 option), and five-star with casters. The document functions as a configuration, height, and finish selection aid to support the pilot rather than as a purchase order or resolution.

It notes the district's roughly nine-year curricular review cycle and a shift toward comprehensive program review encompassing instruction, intervention, assessment, and data, and states the goal of adopting a new resource that fully addresses deep conceptual learning, number sense, and mathematical fluency aligned to the Michigan Math State Standards.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
What it is
- An elementary mathematics materials adoption proposal for the Troy School District, dated March 2023.
- Submitted by Natalie Haezebrouck and Julia Alder.

Rationale
- The district reviews curricular materials on roughly a nine-year cycle; the most recent prior adoption was Middle and High-School Health in 2020.
- The district has updated its review philosophy toward a comprehensive look at programming, including instructional practices, intervention, assessment, and current data, to align curricular, structural, and staffing needs.
- The last elementary math adoption was in 2010.

Drivers
- Better understanding of the Michigan Math State Standards and better-aligned resources now exist.
- Guidance from the National Council of Teachers of Mathematics (NCTM) on best practice continues to develop.
- Teachers have been supplementing current resources with three-act tasks, number sense routines, and additional materials.
- A new resource is desired that fully addresses deep conceptual learning, number sense, and mathematical fluency.

Program review timeline (as charted)
- 2019 Bridges early adopters (Tier 1 focus on conceptual understanding and modeling); 2020 COVID; 2021 review of TSD data and focus on math mindset amid a trend of fewer students proficient over time; 2022-23 continued development.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
Dated March 2023 and submitted by Natalie Haezebrouck and Julia Alder, this proposal makes the case for an elementary mathematics materials adoption in the Troy School District. In its rationale, it notes that the district regularly reviews its curricular materials on roughly a nine-year cycle and that, since the last curricular adoption (Middle and High-School Health in 2020), the district has updated its philosophy regarding curricular review. That updated approach calls for taking a comprehensive look at programming as a whole rather than simply seeking new materials, including understanding instructional practices, intervention, assessment, and current data so that curricular, structural, and staffing needs can be aligned (referenced as Image 1, an Elementary Mathematics Program Review Timeline).

The proposal states that the last elementary math adoption was conducted in 2010, and that much has changed since then both in the field of mathematics and in Troy classrooms. It cites a better understanding of the Michigan Math State Standards, the availability of better-aligned resources for elementary math, and the continued development of learning and guidance around best practice by the National Council of Teachers of Mathematics (NCTM). It observes that in recent years teachers have been supplementing the current resource with approaches such as three-act tasks, number sense routines, and additional materials to address missed opportunities, and that a new resource is desired that fully addresses deep conceptual learning, number sense, and mathematical fluency.

The embedded program review timeline references a sequence of milestones: 2019 Bridges early adopters with a Tier 1 focus on conceptual understanding and modeling; 2020 disruption from COVID; extension of ME and math specialists and support for intensive intervention in math; 2021 review of TSD data with a focus on math mindset, noting a trend of fewer students proficient in math over time; and continued comprehensive math program development, MTSS development, and Math Recovery and Tier 1 research through 2022-23. The extracted text is degraded by OCR noise (long runs of repeated digits), but the substantive content establishes the rationale and historical context supporting the recommended elementary math materials adoption.

Year-to-date statement of revenues and expenditures for Troy School District covering July 1, 2022 through January 31, 2023, presenting actual amounts against the amended annual budget for the general fund, the consolidated debt service funds and several special-revenue funds. At roughly the seven-month point of the fiscal year, the report gives the board a budget-to-actual comparison for financial oversight.

General Fund. Revenues recognized total $76,043,278 against a budget of $179,123,295: local sources $28,387,243 (budget $40,757,126), state sources $42,259,719 (budget $117,707,512), federal sources $492,092 (budget $8,944,348), interdistrict sources $4,904,224 (budget $10,514,309) and transfers in and other $0 (budget $1,200,000). The heavy weighting toward future state aid is normal for mid-year. Expenditures total $78,139,403 against a budget of $179,291,500. Instruction totals $48,236,496 (basic programs $35,117,057, added needs $12,701,577, adult education $417,862). Support services total $29,722,990, including operations and maintenance $7,674,953, pupil support $5,668,731, instructional staff $5,073,104, school administration $4,615,630, central services $2,000,100, pupil transportation $1,842,858, athletics $1,209,396, general administration $840,795 and business services $797,423. Community services expense is $125,716 and debt service $54,200. The result is an interim shortfall of $2,096,125, against a full-year budgeted deficit of $168,205.

Consolidated Debt Service Funds. Revenues total $15,232,238 (local $14,959,798, state $272,440) against a $19,175,000 budget. Expenditures total $1,496,198, essentially all interest ($1,495,430); the $15,965,000 budgeted principal had not yet been paid at January 31, producing an interim surplus of $13,736,040 (full-year budgeted deficit $110,325).

Special-Revenue Funds. The Food Service Fund (520) shows year-to-date revenues of $2,600,118 and expenditures of $2,039,591 (budget $3,916,433 / $3,494,620), reflecting a contracted operation with large purchased-service and food-supply costs and federal meal reimbursement. The Troy Career Center Fund (529) shows revenues and expenditures each of $1,363,385 against a $2,312,350 budget, running at net zero. The Community Service Fund (530) shows revenues of $1,107,743 and expenditures of $1,045,940 (budget $3,043,000 / $2,754,953), including an $800,000 budgeted outgoing transfer not yet made. https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
A board-workshop presentation dated March 21, 2023 summarizing the Middle School Visioning process led by Fielding International, a firm of architects, designers, and educators that partners with schools to align environment, vision, and educational programs so learners can thrive now and in the future. The project's stated objective was to engage students, teachers, building leaders, district staff, specialists, and others in co-creating a shared understanding of current needs and a vision for the future of middle school teaching and learning in Troy, with findings intended to inform and improve the design of new and renovated middle school facilities. The approach was described as student-centered, collaborative, constructive, research-based, and inclusive.

Phase 1 (Discovery) asked "What are our current barriers and constraints and who are we designing for?" and comprised 5 building tours, 6 workshops, and 40+ team members. Work explored the 21st-century learner, characterized as tech-savvy, creative, fast-learning consumers and creators of media who need social-emotional support, along with the supports they need, such as multi-use and comfortable spaces with diverse options, teachers acting as guides, student choice, more movement, respect and trust, and less emphasis on tests and homework. Participants designed a "Day-in-the-Life" charette featuring a sample schedule (start 8:00 a.m., end 3:03 p.m.) with courses such as Architectural Science, Algebra 1, Archery, a Creative Period, World History, P.E., and English, plus course menus across Science, Social Studies, Phys Ed, Math, ELA, and Electives, and architectural ideas including collaborative spaces, ranges of seating, maker spaces, movable walls, and a student lounge.

Phase 2 (Visioning) asked "What are the physical conditions we want to create to support our vision for the future?" through 2 workshops, 40+ team members, and thousands of sticky notes. The proposed mission for a re-imagined middle school included seven aims: provide experiential and authentic learning; strive for engagement and fun; foster cultural competencies; promote social learning and empathy; cultivate future-ready skills; build relationships, community, and connectedness; and encourage healthy risks.

The presentation identified a Top 15 list of design patterns and a Top 5: Learning Community, Transparency, Learning Commons, Variable Seating, and Indoor-Outdoor Connections. Other listed patterns included Teacher Collaboration, Daylighting, STEAM Workshop, Small Group Room, Casual Eating Area, Calming Retreat, Integrating the Arts & Performance, Neighborhood-as-a-school, Outdoor Classroom, and Active Hallway. An emerging "learning ecosystem" concept listed team-board areas with typical sizes: Learning Studio (800 sf), Science Lab (980 sf), Production Commons (600 sf), Special Education & Sensory (500 sf), Restoration & Research Commons (500 sf), Teacher Workshop (350 sf), Small Group Room (100 sf), and Deep Storage (100 sf). Next steps were to integrate insights into the design of Smith Elementary (TMP x FI), provide resources for building leaders and educators to continue exploring best practices, and connect principals with an expert in flexible learning environments.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: A November 1, 2021 memorandum from Assistant Superintendent Rick West to Superintendent Rich Machesky updating Troy's high school start-times initiative, revisited at the April 4, 2023 Board workshop. An administrators' committee, formed under the Board's April 20, 2021 resolution, studied moving to a three-tier transportation system for 2022-2023 but concluded the nationwide bus-driver shortage made success unlikely: the 5-tier system needed 63 drivers (10 vacancies) versus 85 (32 vacancies) for 3-tier, with only 19% of applicants hired. The committee recommended delaying implementation, noting 20 additional buses would need to be purchased in December to proceed.

What it is
- Business Office memorandum dated Monday, November 1, 2021, from Rick West (Assistant Superintendent, Business Services) to Superintendent Dr. Rich Machesky, updating the high school start-times project. Included in the April 4, 2023 Board workshop packet.

Background
- An administrators' committee was formed to recommend new start times for 2022-2023, per the Board resolution passed April 20, 2021.
- Members included principals Michelle Barsh (Martell), Mike Cottone (Troy Union), Jonathan Cross (Baker), Joe Duda (Larson), and Melanie Morey (Barnard); Special Education Director Jessica Carrier; Assistant Superintendent Christine DiPilato; Athletic Director Tim Fulcher; Transportation Manager Kathy Kochanski; assistant principals Kristin Meldrum (Athens) and Brian Zawislak (Troy High); Laura Duzey; Superintendent Machesky; and Rick West.

Key findings
- A three-tier transportation system is the most feasible way to support new bell times, but the nationwide bus-driver shortage is a major obstacle.
- 5-tier system: 63 drivers required, 10 vacancies. 3-tier system: 85 drivers required, 32 vacancies.
- Bus-driver pay: $19.00/hour starting, $24.00/hour maximum.
- Since August 2021: ~3.2 weekly applications, 19% of applicants trained and hired, 10% turnover.

Recommendation
- Delay implementation until success can be assured. Proceeding with 2022-2023 would require purchasing 20 additional buses in December 2021.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
A Business Office memorandum dated Monday, November 1, 2021, from Rick West, Assistant Superintendent for Business Services, to Superintendent Dr. Rich Machesky, titled 'High School Start Times Update,' presented in the April 4, 2023 Board of Education workshop packet. It reports on a committee of administrators established to recommend new school start times for the 2022-2023 school year in alignment with a resolution the Board passed at its April 20, 2021 meeting.

The committee comprised Michelle Barsh (Martell Elementary Principal), Jessica Carrier (Special Education Director), Mike Cottone (Troy Union Elementary Principal), Jonathan Cross (Baker Middle School Principal), Christine DiPilato (Assistant Superintendent, Secondary Instruction), Joe Duda (Larson Middle School Principal), Laura Duzey (Pupil Accounting and Central Enrollment Coordinator), Tim Fulcher (Athletic Director), Kathy Kochanski (Transportation Manager), Rich Machesky (Superintendent), Kristin Meldrum (Athens High School Assistant Principal), Melanie Morey (Barnard Elementary Principal), Rick West (Assistant Superintendent, Business Services), and Brian Zawislak (Troy High Assistant Principal). Members reviewed the Board resolution, survey data, current building schedules, and the high school bell times of other Oakland County districts.

The memo concludes that the most feasible way to support a new bell-time schedule is a three-tier transportation system, but that the nationwide bus-driver shortage undermines confidence in successful implementation. Reported staffing statistics: the current 5-tier system requires 63 drivers and has 10 vacancies, while a 3-tier system would require 85 drivers and have 32 vacancies. Current bus-driver pay is $19.00 per hour starting and $24.00 per hour maximum. Since August 2021, the district averaged 3.2 weekly applications, hired and trained only 19% of applicants, and experienced a 10% turnover rate.

Given these conditions and a lack of confidence in implementation, the committee recommends delaying the new start-time schedule until its success can be assured. The memo cautions that if the Board nonetheless wishes to proceed with a 2022-2023 implementation, the district would need to purchase an additional 20 buses in December (2021) to ensure they arrive before the start of the next school year.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: A December 2, 2021 memorandum from Assistant Superintendent Rick West to Superintendent Rich Machesky analyzing a three-tier busing system with reduced transportation-eligibility distances, presented at the April 4, 2023 Board workshop. Raising minimum walk distances by 0.25 mile would cut eligible riders from 6,995 to 2,675 and buses needed from 75 to 57; a 0.5-mile increase would cut riders to 2,072 and buses to 49. Administration does not recommend these changes because they would require students to cross major roads, and warns the driver shortage would grow to 35 drivers under a 3-tier system.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
What it is
- Business Office memorandum dated December 2, 2021, from Rick West (Assistant Superintendent, Business Services) to Superintendent Rich Machesky, analyzing a three-tier transportation system for modified school start times. Included in the April 4, 2023 Board workshop packet.
- Follow-up to the November 9, 2021 Board workshop, where the Board asked Administration to keep brainstorming and to consider changing transportation-eligibility parameters.

Eligibility scenarios analyzed
- Current: 1.5 miles (HS/MS), 1.0 mile (elementary) - 6,995 eligible riders (HS 2,218; MS 2,038; Elem 2,739).
- +0.25 mile: 1.75 miles (HS/MS), 1.25 miles (elem) - 2,675 riders (down 62%).
- +0.5 mile: 2.0 miles (HS/MS), 1.5 miles (elem) - 2,072 riders (down 70%).

Buses required for a 3-tier system (excluding spares)
- Current eligibility: 75 (48 general ed + 27 special ed).
- +0.25 mile: 57 (30 + 27), saving 18-20 drivers.
- +0.5 mile: 49 (22 + 27), saving 26-28 drivers.
- By tier at current eligibility: 5-tier 55; 4-tier 67; 3-tier 75.

Cautions and options
- Reduced eligibility would force elementary and middle students to cross major roads - not recommended.
- Driver shortage: 13 short for the current 5-tier, rising to 35 short for a 3-tier system; routes would be canceled equitably (excluding special education) when short-staffed.
- Other options: keep the 5-tier system but change the HS-MS-elementary cadence, or eliminate high school transportation.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
A Business Office memorandum dated December 2, 2021, from Rick West, Assistant Superintendent for Business Services, to Superintendent Rich Machesky, addressing high school start times and included in the April 4, 2023 Board of Education workshop packet. It follows the November 9, 2021 Board workshop, at which - after discussing the challenges of a 3-tier transportation system for modified 2022-2023 start times - the Board asked Administration to continue brainstorming while signaling willingness to review transportation-eligibility parameters.

The transportation department modeled a 3-tier system while decreasing transportation eligibility by 0.25 mile and 0.5 mile. Under the 0.25-mile change, middle and high school eligibility would require living at least 1.75 miles from the building and elementary at least 1.25 miles; under the 0.5-mile change, 2.0 miles (secondary) and 1.5 miles (elementary). For the analysis, the restriction against crossing major roads was removed, since keeping it would leave eligibility at the current 1.0/1.5 miles.

Eligible general-education riders by scenario: Current (1.5 miles HS/MS, 1.0 mile elementary) - High Schools 2,218, Middle Schools 2,038, Elementary 2,739, total 6,995. At 1.75/1.25 miles - 1,130, 547, and 998, total 2,675. At 2.0/1.5 miles - 911, 428, and 733, total 2,072.

Buses required for a 3-tier system (excluding spares): current eligibility 48 general-education plus 27 special-education, totaling 75; with the 0.25-mile increase 30 + 27 = 57; with the 0.5-mile increase 22 + 27 = 49. By tier at current eligibility: 5-tier (current) 32 + 23 = 55; 4-tier 40 + 27 = 67; 3-tier 48 + 27 = 75. The 0.25-mile modification cuts ridership eligibility by 62% and reduces drivers needed by 18-20; the 0.5-mile modification cuts eligibility by 70% and reduces drivers by 26-28. Administration would not recommend either, because both would require elementary and middle school students to cross major roads.

The memo reiterates concern about staffing a 3-tier system: the district is short 13 drivers for its current 5-tier operation, a shortage that rises to 35 when planning for a 3-tier system (figures inclusive of 8 standby drivers for a 5-tier and 10 for a 3-tier system). The current shortage already requires the dispatcher, contract manager, and district manager to drive routes occasionally, and additional route combinations were planned following two retirements. The Board had asked how a 3-tier system would be managed with insufficient staffing; Administration's plan would cancel routes equitably (excluding special education routes) - for example, if short 25 drivers, canceling 25 of the 48 general-education routes on a routine basis - with significant operational impact. Other options noted for modifying start times include maintaining a 5-tier system while changing the HS-MS-elementary cadence, or eliminating high school transportation. The memo closes by anticipating continued discussion in planning for the 2022-2023 school year.

Four proposals were opened March 21, 2023; TelSystems' base bid of $252,300.00 was lowest, ahead of Acorn ($270,867.90), Moss Telecom ($284,437.70), and Sound Planning ($330,713.00). The recommended award totals $453,676.00 ($252,300 base plus $201,376 in alternates), with a roughly 10% contingency of $45,000 for a total project cost of $498,676.00.

What it is
Vendor recommendation letter supporting award of the elementary audio-systems RFP.

From / To
From John C. Foster, President, Convergent Technology Partners (contact 810-223-0528), to Beth Soggs, Technology Director, Troy School District. Dated March 22, 2023.

Procurement timeline
RFP #9956 was issued March 3, 2023 and posted to district and state websites; Convergent contacted several viable vendors to build the bidding pool. Sealed bids were accepted and opened March 21, 2023; four proposals were received. All were found compliant on requirements, pricing, technical solution, and terms; TelSystems was the low qualified bidder.

Base bids
- TelSystems: $252,300.00
- Acorn: $270,867.90
- Moss Telecom: $284,437.70
- Sound Planning: $330,713.00

Recommended award
TelSystems at $453,676.00 = $252,300.00 base bid plus $201,376.00 in alternates, plus a roughly 10% contingency of $45,000.00, for a total of $498,676.00.

Solution scope
All buildings receive identical technology: stage/cafeteria systems with ceiling-installed microphones, a performer monitor speaker, Bluetooth, handheld and lavalier wireless mics, new speakers, and a ceiling-mounted camera for live streaming, housed in existing stage cabinets. Buildings with a cafeteria/gym partition get two extra speakers. Gyms get a self-contained system with their own Bluetooth and wireless mics using the stage cabinet's processing. The evaluation team accepted all mandatory and voluntary alternates for parity across buildings; the alternates cost $201,376.00.

Notes
The district and Convergent had prior favorable experience with TelSystems, most recently Rochester Community Schools' similar elementary installations.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
A recommendation letter dated March 22, 2023, addressed to Beth Soggs, Technology Director, Troy School District, from John C. Foster, President of Convergent Technology Partners, regarding Elementary School Audio Systems RFP #9956.

Procurement process: On March 3, 2023, Troy School District issued a Request for Proposal soliciting bids for Elementary School Audio Systems. The RFP was posted to the district and state websites, and Convergent spoke with several viable vendors and directed them to download the RFP and supporting documentation to ensure a good bidding pool. On March 21, 2023, sealed bids were accepted and opened by the district; four proposals were received. All proposals were evaluated for compliance with RFP requirements, pricing, technical solution, and acceptance of terms and conditions; all were found compliant. TelSystems was determined to be the low qualified bidder.

Base bid tabulation: TelSystems $252,300.00; Acorn $270,867.90; Moss Telecom $284,437.70; Sound Planning $330,713.00. The letter notes the district had previously used TelSystems for A/V consultation and small projects with good results, and that Convergent had also worked with the company favorably, most recently on Rochester Community Schools installing similar systems in their elementary schools and across the district.

RFP structure and solution: The RFP was configured as a base bid with multiple alternates to give the district flexibility in choosing the right solution at the right price, recognizing that not all elementary buildings share the same layout or requirements. TelSystems also provided additional voluntary alternates that were technically and financially favorable. The common solution across all buildings includes stage and cafeteria systems with microphones permanently installed in the ceilings, a monitor speaker for performers, Bluetooth connection capability, handheld and lavalier wireless microphones, new speakers, and a ceiling-mounted camera for live streaming of events, all housed in existing stage cabinets. For buildings with a partition between the cafeteria/stage and gymnasium, two additional speakers will be installed to allow opening the partition for larger audiences and for use in stand-alone configuration. Gymnasiums will use the powerful processing system in the stage cabinet to function as a self-contained system with their own Bluetooth and wireless microphone systems operable independently of the main stage system; existing cabinets will be reused where available, and small cabinets added where not.

The evaluation team accepted all mandatory and voluntary alternates to achieve technical and operational parity across all elementary buildings and to replace all failed existing equipment. The cost of these alternates is $201,376.00.

Recommended award: Based on evaluation, interview, and collaboration with TelSystems, Convergent recommends awarding RFP #9956 to the low qualified bidder, TelSystems, in the amount of $453,676.00 ($252,300.00 base bid plus alternates of $201,376.00), with an additional approximately 10% contingency of $45,000.00, for a total of $498,676.00. Foster invites questions at 810-223-0528. The letter was presented as agenda item 2.b at the April 4, 2023 Board of Education Workshop, alongside Director Beth Soggs' transmittal memo, which specifies the expense will be funded from the 2023 Bond Fund.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
A Business Services Update slide presentation delivered April 4, 2023, presenting Amendment 1 to the Troy School District's Special Revenue Funds for the 2022-23 fiscal year. The Special Revenue Funds comprise the Food Service Fund, the Community Service Fund, and the Troy Preschool Fund.

Food Service Fund - Amendment 1 highlights: the contractual obligation has been reconciled; average meal participation is 34%, consistent with pre-pandemic levels, compared with over 50% average participation in 2021-22 when free meals were provided for all students. The fund shows a $535,000 projected surplus, a $2.6 million fund balance, and $1.2 million in anticipated excess fund balance; a spend-down plan has been developed and will be adjusted. Universal breakfast and lunch is noted as the Governor's initiative for 2023-24.

Community Service Fund - Amendment 1 highlights: the fund received $1.98 million in federal Child Care Stabilization funds across three rounds of grants, with rounds 2 and 3 recognized in 2022-23. These funds are non-recurring and flexible, usable for salaries and benefits (including employee bonuses), supplies and equipment, and tuition subsidy for parents. Expenditures were reconciled and adjusted as necessary. The fund shows a $1.5 million projected surplus and a $2.5 million fund balance.

Preschool Fund - Amendment 1 highlights: the fund received $1.0 million in federal Child Care Stabilization funds under the same three-round grant structure (rounds 2 and 3 recognized in 2022-23), likewise non-recurring and flexible for salaries and benefits including employee bonuses, supplies and equipment, and parent tuition subsidy. Expenditures were reconciled and adjusted. The fund shows a $1.1 million projected surplus and a $1.8 million fund balance. Universal Preschool is noted as the Governor's initiative for 2023-24, and 2023-24 enrollment is referenced.

The deck closes with a Budget Schedule slide. The presentation conveys highlights only; the detailed revenue-by-source and expenditure-by-object financial tables for all three funds are provided in the companion 2c Business Services Update PDF presented under the same agenda item (2.c).
